transcript.content: Hello, welcome in. I'm Dr. Smith. Can you tell me what brings you in to see me today?

Well, Dr. Smith, I... I guess my family wanted me to come in because they think I'm just having a hard time letting go, but that's not it at all. It's about the data. I'm a systems analyst, so looking at networks and finding discrepancies is literally what I do for a living, and if anyone would just sit down and look at the files I've compiled, they'd see exactly what I'm seeing. 

It’s about my father’s death. I know everyone keeps telling me the hospital records and those donation emails all line up perfectly—my sister, the hospital administrators, they all say it's just standard procedure and I need to drop it. But when I actually sit down and compare the exact timestamps on the routing headers... and the missing attachments—because you don't just have missing attachments on secure, automated medical emails unless someone actively goes into the system and manually strips them out—it paints a completely different picture. 

And then, on top of the digital trail, when I try to talk to certain community members about it, people who were around when it happened and should want to know the truth, they completely avoid my questions. They won't look me in the eye, they change the subject, or they just stop returning my calls altogether. So, I'm here because my family thinks I need to talk to someone, but honestly, it’s just so obvious to me that someone is hiding what really happened around my father’s death, and I'm the only one actually trying to put the pieces together.
Besides these concerns about your father's death, have you ever heard voices or seen things that other people around you don't seem to hear or see?

No, no, definitely not. I mean, I know why you're asking that—my family probably suggested I'm losing my grip or something, but I don't... I don't hallucinate. I don't hear voices whispering to me or see things that aren't there. My brain just doesn't work that way. 

Like I said, I'm a systems analyst. My entire day, my whole career, really, is built on looking at concrete, empirical data. Zeros and ones. Server logs. When I look at a packet capture, I'm seeing exactly what the network hardware processed at that exact millisecond. There's no room for imagination there, you know? I deal in facts. So when I tell you that the timestamps on the hospital's internal routing headers were altered, I'm not seeing things that aren't there. I'm seeing the actual, physical metadata that someone forgot to scrub from the secondary exchange server. 

I don't need to hear voices because the data is already telling the whole story, if that makes sense. It's just... it's incredibly frustrating because people jump to 'oh, he must be imagining things,' when really, I'm the only one actually opening my eyes and looking at the raw information. I mean, if anyone just took five minutes to look at the hexadecimal output of those supposedly 'standard' PDFs, they'd see exactly what I see, which is real, tangible evidence, not some... some phantom voice in my head.

Before your father's death, would you say you generally had a longstanding pattern of distrusting people's motives or suspecting others were being deceptive with you, or is this level of suspicion something new that started around the time he died?

No, no, definitely not. I mean... I've never been a paranoid person, if that's what you're getting at. Honestly, before all this happened with my dad, I was probably one of the more trusting guys you'd meet. 

I mean, obviously, in my line of work, you're trained to look for errors, right? You look for the bugs, the anomalies in the system. So in a purely professional sense, I guess I've always had a critical eye when it comes to code or network architecture. It's literally my job to say, "Hey, this packet loss doesn't make sense." But with actual people? In my day-to-day life? No, absolutely not. I never walked around thinking my friends or my coworkers or... or random hospital administrators were lying to me. I just lived my life. 

Like, if you asked my team lead at work about how I was before last year, he'd tell you I was always the guy who took people at their word. If someone on the dev team said, "Hey, the server is down because of a power blip," I'd say, "Okay, cool, let's reboot." I wouldn't immediately assume they were secretly sabotaging the mainframe or lying to my face. I didn't have any reason to. 

But this... this situation with my father is entirely different. This isn't me suddenly deciding out of nowhere that humanity is deceptive or that everyone has some hidden agenda. It's just a reaction to the evidence. If the data matched their story—if the timestamps actually aligned with the standard procedures they keep quoting at me—I'd drop it right now. I swear I would. I'd go back to being the exact same guy I was before he died, just doing my job and living my life. But I can't just ignore what's right in front of me on the screen, you know? It's not some deep-seated personality trait where I just distrust people for fun, it's... it's just that the facts they're giving me are mathematically impossible based on the server logs.
Can you tell me exactly how long ago your father passed away, and how soon after his death you began having these specific concerns about the records being falsified?

Well, my father passed away... let's see, it's been about nine months now. Nine months since the actual date of his death. And as for when I started noticing all this... it wasn't immediate, not like the very next day. Right after it happened, I was just... you know, I was grieving. I was helping my sister with the arrangements, dealing with the funeral home, just trying to keep my head above water. 

But then, maybe a few weeks later, I started having to sort through his personal affairs. You know how it is, you have to close out accounts, deal with the estate, cancel subscriptions, all that administrative nightmare that comes after someone dies. And because I'm the one who handles the tech stuff in the family, I was the one who logged into his email to make sure we weren't missing any final bills or important correspondence. 

That's when I first saw the emails from the hospital and the donation organization. At first glance, I was just going to archive them, just file them away in a folder labeled 'Medical' and be done with it. But... I don't know, something about the headers caught my eye. The way the routing information was structured just looked... off. Like, if you're using a standard automated system for sending out bereavement or donation notifications, the SMTP relays follow a very specific, predictable path. But these didn't. 

So I dug a little deeper. I started looking at the raw message source. And that's when I saw the discrepancies in the timestamps. The server hops were showing a negative time delta, which is physically impossible unless the system clock on one of the servers was manually rolled back, or... or someone intercepted the message, altered the payload, and injected it back into the queue with a spoofed timestamp. 

So, to answer your question, it's been going on for about nine months, basically starting just a few weeks after he died when I first opened those records. And ever since then, the more I look, the more I find. It's like pulling a thread on a sweater, you know? Once I saw that first anomaly, I had to look at the PDF attachments, and then I had to look at the metadata on those, and then I had to cross-reference that with the hospital's public-facing SSL certificates... and it just... it all points to the same conclusion. I've been trying to explain this to my sister for months, but she just cuts me off and says I'm obsessing. But I'm not obsessing, I'm just following the data trail that started nine months ago.

Aside from this situation involving your father's death, has anything changed in other areas of your life—like your job performance, sleep, or relationships with friends—since this all started nine months ago?

Honestly, no. I mean, if you looked at my day-to-day life from the outside, you wouldn't see any difference at all. I still go to work every single day. Actually, I'm the lead on a pretty massive legacy database migration right now, which takes up a ton of my focus, and I'm handling all those projects without missing a beat. My sprint velocities at work are exactly where they should be, my boss hasn't had a single complaint. I pay my bills on time, I keep the house clean, I still do my grocery shopping on Sunday mornings... I just keep my completely normal routine. Everything in that regard is totally standard, and I'm functioning exactly like I always have. 

The only thing—and I mean literally the only place where things get tense or where there's any kind of friction—is when I bring up my questions about my father's records with my family or, you know, people in the community who were involved with his estate or the hospital. That's it. 

Like with my sister, I'll just try to sit her down and say, look, just look at this one page of the packet capture, just look at the timestamps on these emails, and she instantly gets angry. She gets incredibly tense and tells me I'm ruining family dinners or that I need to drop it. Or if I try to ask the community liaison about the discrepancies in the donation paperwork, they treat me like I'm being a nuisance or like I'm trying to start a fight. It's incredibly frustrating because I'm just functioning normally, doing my job, paying my mortgage, living my life, but the second I try to share this very real, very documented problem with them, they completely shut me out. So yeah, there's definitely a lot of tension in my relationships with my family right now, absolutely, but it's not because my life is falling apart or my sleep is messed up. It's strictly because they just refuse to engage with the facts I'm putting right in front of them.
